werkzeug.k8-opposition.name: Opposition
werkzeug.k8-opposition.regel: Rule: Chapter 8, rule 2 and “Distant and diagonal opposition”. The kings stand in opposition when they are on one file or rank with one square (direct), three or five squares (distant) between them, or on a diagonal with one or three squares between them. The player who is not to move has the opposition. The app only names opposition moves that hold the result: in king and pawn versus king exactly, with an endgame tablebase; in pure pawn endgames with more pawns, only moves that don't give up a pawn. It names the distant opposition with five squares after the one with three squares and adds “whether that is enough is shown by the key squares”. If no opposition move holds the result, it says what decides instead: the stalemate, the square, a pawn move, the spare tempo or another king move. Gray: the squares between the kings. Gold: the squares on which the king to move takes the opposition and holds the result. Gold arrow: the move that decides instead; red arrow: the move that gives stalemate.
werkzeug.k8-opposition.erklaerung: Endgame: are the kings in opposition, who has it, and which moves take it?
werkzeug.k8-opposition.legende: Gray: the squares between the kings. Gold: the squares on which a king takes the opposition and holds the result. Gold arrow: the move that decides instead; red arrow: the stalemating move.
werkzeug.k8-quadrat.name: Square
werkzeug.k8-quadrat.regel: Rule: Chapter 8, “The rule of the square”. From the passed pawn to the promotion square, toward the side of the enemy king, a square is formed. If the enemy king can step into it when it is his move, he catches the pawn. As in the book, the square always starts at the pawn. Side to move: if the pawn's side is to move, the pawn moves first; then the square shrinks by one rank, and the king must be able to step into the smaller square. Double step: if the pawn stands on its starting square, also one rank further. Gold: the pawn's route; gray: the other sides; the enemy king gold if he catches the pawn, red if the pawn runs through. Caveats according to the chess tip: the rule applies to a single passed pawn that its own king does not help and that nothing stops. Therefore the app gives no verdict when your own king stands in front of or next to the pawn (then key squares and opposition count) and when connected passed pawns protect each other; the king is then gray. A pawn behind a pawn of its own on the same file does not count as a passed pawn of your own. If a pawn becomes a passed pawn with the next move, the app checks its square in the position after that move and names it first.
werkzeug.k8-quadrat.erklaerung: Endgame: does the king catch the passed pawn? The square, with side to move and double step. Tap a passed pawn to select it.
werkzeug.k8-quadrat.legende: Gold arrow: the pawn's route. Gray: the other sides of the square. King gold if he reaches the square, red if not, gray if the rule gives no verdict here.
werkzeug.k8-schluesselfelder.name: Key squares
werkzeug.k8-schluesselfelder.regel: Rule: Chapter 8, “Key squares: where the king wants to go”. Pawn on the 2nd, 3rd or 4th rank: the three squares two ranks in front of it; 5th or 6th rank: the six squares one and two ranks in front of it; rook pawn: the last two squares of the neighboring file. If the king of the pawn's side stands on a key square, he wins, no matter who is to move, as long as the pawn is not lost immediately. Gold: the key squares of your own passed pawns and the king move to get there; red: those of the enemy passed pawns (his king must not get there). Special case 6th rank: whether the pawn reaches the 7th rank without check; if it gets there without check and the pawn's side is to move, the conclusion names the pawn move.
werkzeug.k8-schluesselfelder.erklaerung: Endgame: the key squares of both sides' passed pawns and whether the king occupies or reaches them.
werkzeug.k8-schluesselfelder.legende: Gold: key squares of the passed pawns of {eigen} and the king move to get there. Red: the key squares of {gegner}.
werkzeug.k8-elementarmatt.name: Basic mates
werkzeug.k8-elementarmatt.regel: Rule: Chapter 8, basic mates with queen, rook or two bishops against the lone king. Gray: the box, that is, the squares the king still has left (via squares the strong side does not attack). Gold: moves that give mate at once. Red: moves that give stalemate. Plus, when the strong side is to move: checks that safely shrink the box (driving moves), quiet moves that shrink it (blocking moves, gray arrows), and moves of the blocking piece that leave the box unchanged and keep it out of the king's reach (waiting moves, rook and queen). Facing each other: the kings on one file or rank with one square between them.
werkzeug.k8-elementarmatt.erklaerung: Endgame: queen, rook or two bishops against the king. The app shows the box, the mating moves and the moves that give stalemate.
werkzeug.k8-elementarmatt.legende: Gray: the box and the blocking moves. Gold arrows: mating moves. Red arrows: moves that give stalemate.
opposition.zuegeTitel: Moves with which {farbe} takes the opposition
opposition.lage.direkt: Direct opposition on the {richtung}: one square between them ({zwischen})
opposition.lage.fern: Distant opposition on the {richtung}: {anzahl} squares between them ({zwischen})
opposition.keine: No opposition: the kings are not on the same file, rank or diagonal with one, three or five squares between them.
opposition.merkregel: Rule of thumb: if the number of squares between the kings is odd, the player who has just moved has the opposition.
opposition.hat: {hat} has the opposition: {amZug} is to move and must give way.
opposition.keinZug: No king move takes the opposition now: {farbe} must give way or look for another plan.
opposition.fazitKeine: No opposition, and no move takes it.
schluessel.keinFreibauer: No passed pawn on the board: key squares apply to passed pawns (Chapter 5: no enemy pawn stops them).
schluessel.art.drei: Pawn on rank {reihe}: the three squares two ranks ahead of it, {felder}
schluessel.art.sechs: Pawn on rank {reihe}: the six squares one and two ranks ahead of it, {felder}
schluessel.art.rand: Rook pawn: the last two squares of the neighboring file, {felder}
schluessel.art.keine: Pawn on rank {reihe}: the book names no key squares for this; calculate up to promotion (Rule 6).
schluessel.besetzt: The king on {koenig} stands on a key square: {farbe} wins regardless of who is to move, as long as the pawn is not lost at once.
schluessel.erreichbar: {farbe} to move can occupy a key square: {zuege}.
schluessel.ohneKoenig: Without both kings the situation cannot be judged.
schluessel.abstand: No key square occupied: {farbe}'s king needs {eigen} to reach the nearest one, {gegner}'s king {fremd}. The opposition decides who gets through.
schluessel.randbauer: Rook-pawn exception: if the defending king reaches the corner in time, the position is usually a draw; it is won if the attacking king reaches b7/b8 (g7/g8).
schluessel.sechste.ohneSchach: Special case 6th rank: the pawn reaches the 7th rank without check, and the side with the pawn wins.
schluessel.sechste.mitSchach: Special case 6th rank: the pawn could only reach the 7th rank with check; then the king steps in front of it, and the attacker must give up the pawn or stalemate.
schluessel.sechste.verteidiger: The defender to move places the king diagonally in front of the pawn ({felder}), so that the pawn move comes with check.
schluessel.fazitBesetzt: {farbe}'s king stands on a key square.
schluessel.fazitErreichbar: {farbe} can now occupy a key square: {zuege}.
schluessel.fazitFern: {farbe} cannot reach a key square yet: take the opposition first.
quadrat.keinFreibauer: No passed pawn on the board: the rule of the square applies to passed pawns.
quadrat.zugrecht: {farbe} is to move: after the pawn move, the square shrinks to {von}–{bis}. The king must be able to enter this smaller square with its move.
quadrat.doppelschritt: The pawn is still on its starting square: because of the double step, the square is counted as if it stood one rank further.
quadrat.ohneKoenig: No enemy king on the board.
quadrat.haelt: The king on {koenig} is inside the square or enters it: {farbe} catches the pawn.
quadrat.haeltNicht: The king on {koenig} does not reach the square: the pawn runs through to queen on its own.
quadrat.vorbehalt.blockiert: Caveat: something stands in the pawn's path; calculate concretely.
quadrat.vorbehalt.eigenerKoenig: Caveat: the pawn's own king is nearby and can help; the rule applies to the pawn alone.
quadrat.vorbehalt.weitereFiguren: Caveat: other pieces on the board can give check or block the path; calculate concretely.
quadrat.fazitLaeuft: The pawn on {bauer} runs through: {farbe} does not reach the square.
quadrat.begleitet: The rule of the square does not apply here: the king escorts its pawn – use key squares and opposition.
quadrat.verbunden: The rule of the square only applies to a lone pawn; connected passed pawns protect each other: if the king takes the rear one, the front one runs through.
quadrat.kommend: With the next move {zug} the pawn becomes a passed pawn; the square applies to the position after that.
quadrat.fazitKommendLaeuft: After {zug}, the pawn on {bauer} runs through: {farbe} does not reach the square.
elementarmatt.keins: No basic mate: for that, one side has only its king, and the other has a queen, a rook, two bishops, or bishop and knight.
elementarmatt.art.zweiLaeufer: {farbe}: king and two bishops against king
elementarmatt.art.laeuferSpringer: {farbe}: king, bishop and knight against king
elementarmatt.patt: Stalemate: the king is not in check and has no move.
elementarmatt.kasten: The box: the king on {koenig} has {anzahl} square(s) left (gray): {felder}.
elementarmatt.gegenueber: The kings face each other: now a check drives the king back one rank, and on the edge it is mate.
elementarmatt.nichtGegenueber: The kings do not face each other yet: bring your king closer or make a waiting move.
elementarmatt.schwachAmZug: {farbe} to move: the king stays in the box.
elementarmatt.treibezuege: Driving moves (check, the box gets smaller): {zuege}.
elementarmatt.abwartezuege: Waiting moves (the box stays, the piece out of reach): {zuege}.
elementarmatt.koenigNach: No mate, no blocking move and no driving move: the king moves up.
elementarmatt.methode.dame: Box method: the queen cuts off a rank or file and locks the king in a box; your own king moves up. Only when it is close enough does the queen make the box smaller; on the edge it mates, protected by the king. Close the last rank only when the king is ready, or stalemate threatens.
elementarmatt.methode.turm: Three steps: the rook blocks and stays far away from the king; your own king steps opposite the enemy king; if it is your move while the kings do not face each other yet, a waiting move helps. If the king attacks the rook, the rook moves to the other end of its rank.
elementarmatt.methode.zweiLaeufer: Side by side, the bishops form a wall of two diagonals; push the wall forward step by step, let the king follow, and drive the enemy king into a corner. At the end one bishop gives check while the other covers the escape square.
elementarmatt.methode.laeuferSpringer: Bishop and knight: much harder, only in a corner of the bishop's color, up to more than 30 moves. The book recommends learning it only once the other basic endgames are secure.
regeln.fazit: Six rules, checked against this position.
regeln.fazitWeg: Rule 1: the king reaches {ziel} safely in {zuege}.
regeln.r1.ohneKoenig: No king of your own on the board.
regeln.r1.steht: The king stands on {koenig} (rank {reihe}, counted from its own side).
regeln.r1.damen: Queens are still on the board: the king stays behind its pawns until checks and mating threats can no longer punish it (Chapter 1).
regeln.r1.keinWeg: No safe route to a goal (key squares or center): every square on the way is attacked or occupied.
regeln.r1.amZiel: The king is already at its goal ({ziel}).
regeln.r2.hat: {farbe} has the opposition (the side that is not to move).
regeln.r2.nehmen: These moves take the opposition now: {zuege}.
regeln.r2.keine: No opposition, and no king move takes it.
regeln.r3.entfernt: Second weakness: the outside passed pawn {bauern}, far from the enemy king. It decoys the king while yours wins pawns on the other side.
regeln.r3.rennen: Both sides have passed pawns: if they race, every tempo counts (pawn race, four questions).
regeln.r3.geduld: No passed pawn: improve your position, restrict the enemy king and wait for a second weakness.
regeln.r4.mehr: {farbe} is {vorsprung} up: trade pieces, keep the pawns. Before trading the last piece, calculate the pawn endgame.
regeln.r4.weniger: {farbe} is {rueckstand} down: trade pawns, keep pieces. Without pawns the opponent often cannot win.
regeln.r4.gleich: Material equal: trade only if the resulting endgame makes your task easier.
regeln.r5.koenigPassiv: The king {koenig} still stands behind the pawns: in the endgame it belongs up front.
regeln.r5.turmPassiv: The rook {turm} has few squares: look for counterplay instead of only guarding (Chapter 9: checks from the side and from behind).
regeln.r6.kontrolliert: (the promotion square is attacked by the opponent)
regeln.r6.keiner: No passed pawn: calculating to promotion is not on the agenda yet.
opposition.zugFuenf: {zug} takes the {lage} – whether that is enough is shown by the key squares
opposition.pruefung.exakt: Checked exactly with the endgame tablebase for king and pawn against king: the app lists only moves that keep the result.
opposition.pruefung.bauernverlust: With several pawns, the app only checks whether the move gives up a pawn; whether it wins only calculation can show.
opposition.grund.patt: Here it is not the opposition that decides but stalemate: {zuege} gives stalemate, and no move wins.
opposition.grund.quadrat: Here it is not the opposition that decides but the square: with {zuege} the king steps into the square and catches the pawn.
opposition.grund.quadratLaeuft: Here it is not the opposition that decides but the square: after {zuege} the enemy king can no longer reach the square.
opposition.grund.bauernzug: Here it is not the opposition that decides but the pawn move {zuege}.
opposition.grund.reservetempo: Here it is not the opposition that decides but the spare tempo {zuege}: after it, {gegner} has to move the king and gives up a pawn.
opposition.grund.koenigszug: Here it is not the opposition that decides but another king move: {zuege}. The key squares show where the king wants to go.
opposition.grund.remis: Here it is not the opposition that decides: no move wins, the position is a draw.
opposition.grund.verloren: Here it is not the opposition that decides: every move loses, the side with the pawns gets through.
opposition.grund.bauernverlust: Here it is not the opposition that decides: every king move that takes it gives up a pawn. Look for a spare tempo or calculate concretely.
elementarmatt.sperrzuege: Blocking moves (quiet, the box gets smaller): {zuege} (gray arrows).
werkzeug.k9-turmbegriffe.name: Rook endgame
werkzeug.k9-turmbegriffe.regel: Rule: Chapter 9, “Three terms for every rook endgame”. The terms apply to rook and one pawn versus rook (and rook versus pawn); if there are several pawns on the board, the tool refers you to the recognition pattern. The attacker is the side with the most advanced passed pawn. Cutting off: the attacker's rook stands on a file (or rank) between the defending king and the pawn; the files in between are counted, and from three on it is often enough to win. Checking distance: the files between the defending rook and the pawn, at least three. Short and long side: the files next to the pawn up to the edge; the defender's king belongs on the short side, the rook on the long side. If the defending king stands in front of the pawn and the attacking king is not yet in front of its pawn, checking distance and sides don't apply: then Philidor applies (rook on the defender's 3rd rank, after the pawn move give checks from behind). Gray: blocking line and checking distance; the defender's king and rook gold if they are placed correctly, otherwise red.
werkzeug.k9-turmbegriffe.erklaerung: Rook endgame with a passed pawn: is the king cut off, does the rook have checking distance, are king and rook on the right side?
werkzeug.k9-turmbegriffe.legende: Gray arrows: blocking line and checking distance. The defender's king and rook gold if they are placed correctly, otherwise red.
werkzeug.k9-erkennungsbilder.name: Recognition pattern
werkzeug.k9-erkennungsbilder.regel: Rule: Chapter 9, review table. The app goes through the recognition questions from top to bottom: rook and pawn versus rook (Lucena: pawn on the 7th rank, king in front of it, enemy king cut off to the side; Vancura: far-advanced rook pawn with the rook in front of it; Philidor: defending king in front of the pawn; otherwise short side), rook versus pawn, rook endgame with several pawns (rook behind the passed pawn), queen versus pawn (bishop pawn or rook pawn, stalemate after the capture), queen versus queen, rook versus bishop (corner), bishop endgames (same or opposite colors, wrong bishop; with opposite-colored bishops the app counts the passed pawns: two that are at least three files apart are called separated and usually win, close or connected ones allow a fortress draw), bishop versus knight (wings), knight. Exact (E) when the book's standard position has been reached, otherwise approximation (N) with the plan from the table.
werkzeug.k9-erkennungsbilder.erklaerung: Endgame deep dive: which pattern from the table is on the board, and which plan follows from it?
werkzeug.k9-erkennungsbilder.legende: The key square of the pattern, such as the passed pawn or a king: gold if it speaks for the plan, red if it endangers it, gray for orientation.
turmbegriffe.titel: Three terms for the rook endgame
turmbegriffe.keinsTitel: No rook endgame with a passed pawn
turmbegriffe.keins: The three terms apply to rook endgames with a passed pawn; here the rook or the passed pawn is missing.
turmbegriffe.abschneiden.ja: The rook {turm} blocks a file between the king {koenig} and the pawn: {dazwischen} in between (gray arrow).
turmbegriffe.abschneiden.nein: The king {koenig} is not cut off: no rook blocks a file or rank between it and the pawn.
turmbegriffe.abschneiden.reicht: Rule of thumb: from three files on, it is often enough to win.
turmbegriffe.abschneiden.wenig: Rule of thumb: the more files in between, the better for the attacker; from three on, it is often enough.
turmbegriffe.schachdistanz.keinTurm: The defender has no rook: no checking distance to measure.
turmbegriffe.schachdistanz.linien: Between the rook {turm} and the pawn {bauer}: {linien} (needed: {soll}).
turmbegriffe.schachdistanz.reicht: That is enough for its checks: if the king walks toward it, the king leaves its pawn.
turmbegriffe.schachdistanz.zuNah: Too close: the king walks toward the rook without leaving its pawn, and the checks stop.
turmbegriffe.seiten.links: Next to the pawn {bauer}: on the left {links} files to the edge (short side), on the right {rechts} (long side).
turmbegriffe.seiten.linksEins: Next to the pawn {bauer}: on the left 1 file to the edge (short side), on the right {rechts} (long side).
turmbegriffe.seiten.rechts: Next to the pawn {bauer}: on the right {rechts} files to the edge (short side), on the left {links} (long side).
turmbegriffe.seiten.rechtsEins: Next to the pawn {bauer}: on the right 1 file to the edge (short side), on the left {links} (long side).
turmbegriffe.seiten.gleich: Next to the pawn {bauer}: both sides are equally long ({links} files).
turmbegriffe.koenigAuf.kurz: The king {koenig} is on the short side (correct).
turmbegriffe.koenigAuf.lang: The king {koenig} is on the long side: it belongs on the short one.
turmbegriffe.koenigAuf.gleich: The king {koenig} stands next to the pawn; both sides are equally long.
turmbegriffe.koenigAuf.bauernlinie: The king {koenig} is on the pawn's file (in front of it: Philidor).
turmbegriffe.turmAuf.kurz: The rook {turm} is on the short side: it belongs on the long one, with checking distance.
turmbegriffe.turmAuf.lang: The rook {turm} is on the long side (correct).
turmbegriffe.turmAuf.gleich: The rook {turm} stands next to the pawn; both sides are equally long.
turmbegriffe.turmAuf.bauernlinie: The rook {turm} is on the pawn's file (behind or in front of it).
turmbegriffe.fazit: {angreifer} attacks with the pawn {bauer}; the defending king is {abgeschnitten}.
bilder.titel: Recognition patterns of the endgame deep dive
bilder.keins: No pattern from the table fits: the recognition questions apply to rook, queen, bishop and knight endgames with little material.
bilder.verweis: More on this in the book: Chapter 9, “Review: the recognition patterns”.
bilder.fazitStandard: {name}: the book's standard position is on the board.
bilder.fazitBild: {name}: the pattern, but not yet the standard position.
bilder.philidor.name: Philidor position
bilder.philidor.frage: The defending king stands in front of the pawn.
bilder.philidor.plan: The rook blocks the rank directly in front of the pawn so that the attacking king cannot come forward. If the pawn steps onto that rank, the rook switches behind and gives check after check.
bilder.philidor.sperren: The rook blocks rank {reihe} from the side, far from the enemy king
bilder.philidor.hinten: The pawn is on rank {reihe}: the rook switches behind and gives checks
bilder.kurzeSeite.name: King to the short side
bilder.kurzeSeite.frage: The defending king has been pushed away from the promotion square.
bilder.kurzeSeite.plan: The king goes to the side of the pawn with fewer files, the rook to the other. At least three files between rook and pawn, so that the checks from the side work.
bilder.kurzeSeite.turm: Rook on the long side with checking distance {linien} (needed: {soll})
bilder.lucena.name: Lucena position
bilder.lucena.frage: The pawn is on the seventh rank, its king in front of it, the other king cut off to the side.
bilder.lucena.plan: Building a bridge: first push the other king one more file away with a rook check, then put the rook on the fourth rank. The king leaves the promotion square in a zigzag; when checks come from the side, the rook steps in between, defended.
bilder.lucena.lage: The enemy king stands {linien} beside the pawn, cut off by the rook
bilder.vancura.name: Vancura position
bilder.vancura.frage: A far-advanced rook pawn, with the attacker's rook in front of it.
bilder.vancura.plan: The defender's rook attacks the pawn from the side and gives check from there. The king waits on g7 or h7 (with the h-pawn on a7 or b7).
bilder.vancura.turm: The defending rook attacks the pawn from the side
bilder.turmGegenBauer.name: Rook against pawn
bilder.turmGegenBauer.frage: Is the king of the pawn's side cut off, and which king arrives in time?
bilder.turmGegenBauer.plan: Cut the king off with the rook and count the moves to promotion. The defender keeps underpromotion in mind. Two connected pawns on the sixth rank are stronger than the rook.
bilder.turmGegenBauer.abgeschnitten: The king of the pawn's side is cut off ({dazwischen} in between)
bilder.turmGegenBauer.frei: The king of the pawn's side is not cut off
bilder.turmGegenBauer.rennen: Race: the pawn needs {schritte}, its king is {angreifer} from the pawn, the rook's king {verteidiger} from the promotion square
bilder.mehrbauern.name: Rook endgame with several pawns
bilder.mehrbauern.frage: How active is the rook, and is it behind a passed pawn?
bilder.mehrbauern.plan: Make the rook active, attack a second weakness, then trade into a won pawn endgame. An extra pawn on just one wing, say four against three, often does not win.
bilder.mehrbauern.hinterEigen: The rook {turm} is behind its own passed pawn {bauer} (gold)
bilder.mehrbauern.hinterFremd: The rook {turm} is behind the enemy passed pawn {bauer} (red)
bilder.mehrbauern.keiner: No rook is behind a passed pawn
bilder.dameGegenBauer.name: Queen against pawn
bilder.dameGegenBauer.frage: Is it a bishop pawn or a rook pawn, and would the capture be stalemate?
bilder.dameGegenBauer.plan: The queen forces the king in front of its pawn with checks. In every pause your own king moves one step closer, until the pawn falls with check.
bilder.dameGegenBauer.laeufer: Bishop pawn {bauer}: stalemate alert, often a draw (Fig. 9.31)
bilder.dameGegenBauer.rand: Rook pawn {bauer}: stalemate alert, often a draw
bilder.dameGegenBauer.mitte: Pawn {bauer} on the b-, d-, e- or g-file: the queen wins
bilder.dameGegenBauer.schlagGeht: Capturing on {bauer} does not give stalemate
bilder.dameGegenDame.name: Queen against queen
bilder.dameGegenDame.frage: Can the defender give perpetual check?
bilder.dameGegenDame.plan: The defender calculates every check. The attacker first brings his king into shelter.
bilder.laeufer.name: Bishop endgame
bilder.laeufer.frage: Same-colored or opposite-colored bishops? A wrong bishop? Can the passed pawns be blockaded?
bilder.laeufer.plan: The defender builds a fortress: he blockades on the squares of the color that the enemy bishop never reaches.
bilder.laeufer.gleich: Same-colored bishops: the passed pawn decides
bilder.laeufer.ungleichGetrennt: Opposite-colored bishops, separated passed pawns {bauer} and {partner}: usually won, because king and bishop cannot blockade on both wings at once
bilder.laeufer.zaehlen: Rule of the book: count the passed pawns that cannot be blockaded
bilder.laeufer.falsch: Wrong bishop: the bishop does not control the promotion square {ecke}, and the king is in the corner: draw
bilder.laeufer.falschFern: Wrong bishop: the bishop does not control the promotion square {ecke}; a draw if the king reaches the corner
bilder.springer.name: Knight endgame
bilder.springer.frage: Can the passed pawns be blockaded?
bilder.springer.plan: The knight does not work from a distance: count the moves it needs to reach the decisive square.
bilder.springer.tempi: Knight: count the tempi to the promotion square
bilder.laeuferGegenSpringer.name: Bishop against knight
bilder.laeuferGegenSpringer.frage: Are there pawns on both wings or only on one?
bilder.laeuferGegenSpringer.plan: With pawns on both wings the bishop is stronger, because it switches sides quickly. On one wing the knight is often better.
bilder.laeuferGegenSpringer.beide: Pawns on both wings: advantage bishop
bilder.laeuferGegenSpringer.einer: Pawns on only one wing: often advantage knight
bilder.turmGegenLaeufer.name: Rook against bishop
bilder.turmGegenLaeufer.frage: In which corner is the king of the bishop's side?
bilder.turmGegenLaeufer.plan: The bishop's side flees into the corner whose color the bishop does not have.
bilder.turmGegenLaeufer.richtig: The corner {ecke} is the opposite color to the bishop: the right corner
bilder.turmGegenLaeufer.falsch: The corner {ecke} is the bishop's color: the wrong corner
turmbegriffe.abschneiden.reihe: The rook {turm} blocks rank {reihe}: the king {koenig} can no longer reach the pawn (gray arrow).
turmbegriffe.seiten.rand: Rook pawn {bauer}: there is only one side next to it; the defending king waits on g7/h7 (with the h-pawn a7/b7), see Vancura.
turmbegriffe.seiten.nurEinTurm: Short and long side apply to rook and pawn against rook; here only one side has a rook.

werkzeug.k11-phase.name: Phase
werkzeug.k11-phase.regel: Rule: Chapter 12, thinking routine step 1, and Chapter 8, “When does the endgame begin”. Endgame if the four check questions mostly (at least three) come out yes: queens off the board; both kings safe from a mating attack (without queens and without a mate threat in one move); your own king can reach the center via unattacked squares; the pawns decide. Opening as long as the opening goals have not been met; the app reads this as development: middlegame as soon as one side is developed (at most one minor piece on its starting square, as in the book at Fig. 12.1) or the piece material is unequal by at least one minor piece; opening as long as both sides still have two or more minor pieces at home. A king that has not castled is a question of king safety, not of the phase. The pawns decide: a passed pawn, or a pawn majority with little piece material (at most 13 points per side without pawns). One extra rule that does not come from the book and is labeled as such in the display: endgame as soon as each side has at most 13 points in pieces and pawns besides the king (Speelman), even with queens on the board. The phase is the same for both sides; the question about the king in the center is asked for the side to move. For each phase, the tools from the summary page; for the example games from Chapter 11, the row of the book's table. Approximation. Gold: in the endgame, the route of the king of the side to move into the center.

werkzeug.k12-kandidaten.name: Candidates
werkzeug.k12-kandidaten.regel: Rule: Chapter 12, thinking routine steps 2 to 4. Step 2: candidates in calculation order (at most two each of checks, captures without loss, moves with a new threat), plus the next book move as a quiet candidate; if the opponent threatens mate in one, a move that parries it (defense against a threat, preferably without losing a piece and while developing a minor piece); if nothing is forcing, the card names the tool for the phase. In check, all defensive moves are the candidates (move the king, capture the attacker, interpose; glossary “Check”), the book move first. Step 3: for each candidate, the opponent's strongest reply in the order mate, winning capture, check, threat, red for the first candidate; if the replying piece then attacks two targets, it is called a fork (Chapter 7, W6). Step 4: material balance after candidate and reply; then the best candidate. If a candidate is answered with mate, it is ruled out regardless of material; if it gives mate itself, it is the best. If your own king then stands in the open (see Safety check), the card says so too. Approximation, one move deep; the calculation until things are quiet is done by the Quiet tool (Chapter 7).
werkzeug.k12-kandidaten.erklaerung: Thinking routine, steps 2 to 4: collect candidates, the strongest reply to each candidate, balance afterwards; the engine evaluates each candidate and says whether it holds, improves or worsens the position.

werkzeug.k12-sicherheitsblick.name: Safety check
werkzeug.k12-sicherheitsblick.regel: Rule: Chapter 12, safety check before moving, three questions about the move being checked (the next book move or a move of your own via Move): is my king safe afterwards (mate in one, king in the open, free neighboring squares, the opponent's checks)? Can the opponent capture the moved piece at once (exchange balance)? Do I allow a check or even a mate? King in the open: it has left its back rank, stands without a pawn shield (fewer than two of its own pawns directly in front of it or one square further) and the opponent attacks at least two neighboring squares; this only applies as long as the opponent has a queen (in the endgame the king belongs in the center, Chapter 8). Example Fig. 12.3: 3... f5. Gold: the move; red: the capture of the piece, the checks allowed and the attacked neighboring squares.

phase.ist.zuHause: Opening: not both sides are developed and castled yet, and little has happened: hardly any exchanges, back ranks still occupied, the camps still apart.
phase.ist.beideFertig: Middlegame: both sides are developed (at most one minor piece still on its starting square) and have castled, as the glossary requires; the endgame questions do not yet mostly answer yes.
phase.ist.abtausch: Middlegame: four or more pieces have been exchanged (at most ten left apart from kings and pawns); the opening is over even if development is not complete.
phase.ist.grundreihe: Middlegame: one side has largely left its back rank (fewer than four of its own men on it); the opening is over even if development is not complete.
phase.ist.kontakt: Middlegame: the pieces of both sides already stand close together, partly deep in the opponent's camp; the fight has begun even if development is not complete.
phase.ist.damenlos: Middlegame: the queens are off and the endgame questions mostly answer yes, but plenty of material is still on the board (more than 13 points for one side). This is a queenless middlegame.
phase.ist.glossarMittelspiel: Middlegame: both sides are developed (at most one minor piece still on its starting square) and have castled, as the glossary requires; the endgame questions do not yet mostly answer yes.

gegner.kiki: Just for fun: Kiki often plays any move at all, without a plan.
gegner.onkel-otto: Just for fun: Onkel Otto often plays any move at all, without a plan.
gegner.tante-hilde: Just for fun: Tante Hilde often plays any move at all, without a plan.
gegner.bodo: Just for fun: Bodo often plays any move at all, without a plan.
gegner.tom: Tom has only just learned how the pieces move and still charges your king with everything he has. He forgets his own king almost every time.
gegner.marie: Marie likes to arrange her pieces neatly, as if tidying a room. She usually notices what her opponent threatens only once the piece is already gone.
gegner.oma-erna: Grandma Erna loves a little fork and cheers out loud when she finds one. Pawns and endgames bore her, so she tends to leave things hanging there.
gegner.luis: Luis covers everything twice over and moves very slowly. Even so, a piece keeps slipping away from him, because looking is not the same as securing.
gegner.clara: Clara brings her queen out on move two and sends her on a grand tour. Something usually gets lost on the way, but the journey was lovely.
gegner.onkel-bernd: Uncle Bernd trades off whatever he can because he likes endgames. Until then, though, he gives away a pawn more often than he would like.
gegner.emma: Emma got her chess set for her birthday last week and is trying everything once. Sometimes a plan works, sometimes she remembers halfway through a move that she meant to do something else entirely.
gegner.opa-kurt: Grandpa Kurt would rather look out of the window than at the board, telling stories about his chess club back in the sixties. He almost always overlooks quiet moves, and now and then finds a beautiful one.
gegner.frau-schulz: Mrs Schulz plays during her lunch break and is in a hurry. She moves before you have finished yours, and only afterwards notices what was actually under attack.
gegner.lotte: Lotte collects pieces the way other children collect shells. Every pawn left standing goes into her tin, even if her queen is in danger right then.
gegner.henry: Henry wants to deliver mate, and right now. Check, check, check, and when it doesn't work, his own king is suddenly the one in trouble.
gegner.moritz: Moritz has read that you develop your pieces toward the centre, and he sticks to it. Everything that happens afterwards surprises him.
gegner.derya: Derya spots a fork faster than her own mistake. She strikes wherever something flashes and hopes it will work out.
gegner.herr-krause: Mr Krause castles early, builds a fence of pawns and waits. He doesn't like attacking, but while waiting he happily overlooks a threat.
gegner.lina: Lina can't be bothered to castle and prefers to march her pawns forward. Her king stays in the middle and wonders what is going on.
gegner.jakob: Jakob likes trading everything off and enjoys endgames most. Before that he often drops a pawn, but it doesn't bother him much.
gegner.rolf: Rolf is full of beautiful ideas and loves playing the spectacular move. Sadly he rarely sees the quiet one that wins.
gegner.herr-wolff: Mr Wolff plays without preferences and without hurry, just as it comes. His mistakes are those of a beginner, no more and no less.
gegner.pia: Pia loves her queen and attacks with her as soon as the path is clear. Once you chase the queen away, Pia's plan is usually over.
gegner.felix: Felix knows a few openings by heart and comes out of the first ten moves well. After that he gets unsure and prefers quiet moves.
gegner.yusuf: Yusuf likes calculating short combinations and strikes when he sees one. Pawn structures mean nothing to him, and neither do endgames.
gegner.ronja: Ronja defends patiently and without frills. She waits until you try something and keeps playing solidly until then.
gegner.svenja: Svenja storms forward dreaming of the big sacrifice. Sometimes it works, more often a move she didn't see is missing at the end.
gegner.philipp: Philipp counts pawns like money and likes to trade when he is ahead. He almost never declines an offered pawn.
gegner.frau-albrecht: Mrs Albrecht likes to play elegantly and looks for the move that looks like something. Now and then that costs her the simple move that would have been better.
gegner.ella: Ella plays a balanced game without preferences, like most players of her strength. A reliable yardstick for whether you are improving.
gegner.erik: Erik moves fast and attacks even faster. He sees your king, not your threat, and that makes him as dangerous as he is vulnerable.
gegner.dennis: Dennis has a plan, places his pieces well and avoids the mess. Tactical tricks surprise him, especially the small ones.
gegner.leyla: Leyla sees tactics the way others see colours: instantly. In quiet positions she loses the thread, and in the endgame her interest.
gegner.mara: Mara secures everything first, then thinks about what she actually wants. You rarely beat her quickly, but often slowly.
gegner.simon: Simon plays boldly forward and looks for the beautiful combination. If it isn't there, he plays it anyway.
gegner.opa-heinz: Grandpa Heinz stumbles out of the opening, but in the endgame he knows every trick. Don't trade too early, that is where he feels at home.
gegner.holger: Holger plays thoroughly solid chess without preferences. He makes the usual mistakes of his level, and exactly as often as a human would.
gegner.lars: Lars is Holger's twin at the board: balanced, patient, predictable. Beat them both and you have truly understood this level.
gegner.katrin: Katrin attacks with her queen in front and doesn't like sending her home. Survive the king attack and she gets nervous.
gegner.marco: Marco knows the theory and plays the opening straight from the book. Once the book ends, he prefers quiet paths.
gegner.frau-romero: Mrs Romero strikes whenever material is up for grabs and happily calculates a line for it. She never gives a pawn away for free.
gegner.nele: Nele stands firm as a wall and waits for your mistake. She rarely attacks, but she forgives even more rarely.
gegner.johanna: Johanna leaves her king in the centre and prefers to storm forward with her pawns. It looks wild, and it is.
gegner.frau-demir: Mrs Demir trades off whatever bothers her opponent and heads for the endgame with a clear plan. She would rather avoid tactical traps than set them.
gegner.jana: Jana plays a balanced game, but she likes dreaming of the elegant solution. The sober move comes second with her.
gegner.luca: Luca has studied many openings and knows early what he wants. The longer the game goes, the more often he loses the thread.
gegner.guenter: Günter moves briskly and likes to attack without checking for long. One slip in the rush and his game tips over; before that he is unpleasant to face.
gegner.herr-kuehn: Mr Kühn plans move by move and brings every piece to its best square. Only when things get sharp does he sometimes look too late.
gegner.igor: Igor takes what is on the board and calculates it through. Against him every undefended pawn costs a pawn immediately.
gegner.miriam: Miriam defends with a cool head and solid play. She makes little fuss, but she also makes few mistakes.
gegner.samira: Samira plays forward and loves the sacrifice that rips the position open. Whether it is sound she checks afterwards.
gegner.herr-vogel: Mr Vogel trades pieces and looks forward to the endgame, where he plays best. He can be beaten in the opening, hardly at all afterwards.
gegner.herr-hartmann: Mr Hartmann knows the theory deep into the line and plays a balanced game. In the middlegame his confidence sometimes deserts him.
gegner.david: David plays universally and likes to find the beautiful move. He overlooks the inconspicuous alternative more often than is good for him.
gegner.frau-sommer: Mrs Sommer attacks and likes to leave her king in the centre to save time. Usually she is faster, sometimes not.
gegner.herr-lorenz: Mr Lorenz plays cautiously and positionally, every piece safe, every pawn covered. You have to unsettle him; nothing happens by itself.
gegner.defne: Defne calculates fast and deep and finds the tactics others miss. She doesn't like quiet endgames, and it shows.
gegner.amaya: Amaya defends solidly and without haste, every piece protected, every pawn in its place. To beat her you need a plan that spans twenty moves.
gegner.elias: Elias charges in with his queen leading the way and looks for the direct route to the king. If your position holds, his queen eventually runs out of targets.
gegner.frau-wagner: Mrs Wagner trades off whatever she dislikes and steers with a clear plan into an endgame she knows better than you. She would rather sidestep tactical traps than set them.
gegner.fiona: Fiona plays a balanced game and likes to look for the elegant move, even when the plain one would do. That is exactly where you can catch her.
gegner.juna: Juna knows the theory deep into the sidelines and plays without preferences. She is young, but at the board you only notice it in her pace.
gegner.doktor-falk: Doctor Falk attacks before his king is safe and has usually calculated it through. Only every few games does the calculation fail.
gegner.gm-novak: GM Novak builds the position move by move with a grand plan, every piece on its best square. To beat him you have to disrupt the plan early.
gegner.trainer-maier: Coach Maier calculates quickly and strikes as soon as he spots tactics. Afterwards he likes to explain what you should have done, and in his haste he occasionally misses something himself.
gegner.im-becker: IM Becker defends solidly and without preferences, with a surgeon's calm. He waits for the one mistake, and he waits patiently.
gegner.wgm-tanaka: WGM Tanaka plays forward and loves the sacrifice that rips the position open. Usually it is correct, and if not, she has already worked it out before you can exploit it.
gegner.frau-prof-reich: Prof. Reich trades pieces and looks forward to the endgame, where she plays with a scientist's patience. Prevent the trades, or the game is decided.
gegner.gm-okoro: GM Okoro knows the theory down to the twentieth sideline and plays a balanced, secure game. You have to lure him out of the book.
gegner.im-lindgren: IM Lindgren plays solidly and without preferences, with a feel for safe squares. She waits until the position is ripe, and then it is too late.
gegner.ole: Ole goes forward and attacks the king, and precisely so. His courage is calculated, not guessed.
gegner.mats: Mats plays cautiously and positionally, every piece safe, every pawn protected. He almost never makes mistakes, and you have to shake him out of his calm.
gegner.arjun: Arjun calculates like a machine and plays tactics almost flawlessly. His only weakness: he likes it when things get sharp.
gegner.nora: Nora defends calmly and precisely and only attacks once nothing can go wrong anymore. Her mistakes can be counted on one hand.
gegner.melek: Melek pushes forward and attacks the king as soon as a file opens up. Her courage is calculated, and she stays dangerous even against a calm defence.
gegner.tarik: Tarik likes to trade and masters the endgame like an old hand. Whatever you don't take from him in the opening, he takes back there.
gegner.bastian: Bastian knows the theory deep into the sidelines and plays a balanced, secure game. You have to lure him out of the book, and that rarely works.
gegner.oma-ilse: Grandma Ilse has played for sixty years and still looks for the beautiful move. She finds it almost every time, and her rare mistakes are those of a dreamer.
gegner.fm-duarte: FM Duarte attacks the king wherever he finds it and hardly makes a mistake. A win against him is a real achievement.
gegner.im-kraft: IM Kraft plays positionally and knows his theory, with the accuracy of an engine. He waits until you try something.
gegner.opa-walter: Grandpa Walter moves fast and calculates tactics like a machine, because he practically never errs. Only his taste for haste gives you any chance at all.
gegner.wim-okafor: WIM Okafor defends practically flawlessly and only attacks once everything is safe. The strongest wall in this app.
gegner.frau-hoffmann: Mrs Hoffmann leaves her king where it stands and attacks with everything she has. That sounds risky, but she calculates almost flawlessly.
gegner.gm-ivanova: GM Ivanova simplifies without error and wins the endgame with an engine's precision. You have to force the decision early.
gegner.gm-berglund: GM Berglund plays everything and plays it almost perfectly. Anyone who beats him could probably write this book too.
gegner.herr-yilmaz: Mr Yılmaz plays everything and likes to look for the beautiful move that even an engine finds only at second glance. His few mistakes are those of a dreamer.

rueckblick.zweigStrafe: This is how the mistake is punished:
rueckblick.balkenInfo: The bar to the left of the board shows who stands better: the further the light part reaches, the better White stands; in the middle the position is equal. The number is the engine's evaluation from White's point of view, roughly in pawns: +1 means about a pawn better, −2 two pawns worse, “M3” mate in three moves. An extra piece often shows as 5 to 7 instead of 3 as in the book's table of values. That is why the card for a mistake gives the winning chance before and after.
spielstaerke.erklaerung: Accuracy: 100% means every move was the best. One serious mistake counts for more than many good moves. The estimated playing strength says which Lichess rating people roughly have who play the way you did in this game. A single game is not very precise, which is why a range is shown; over several games it gets narrower (card “Your playing strength” under Play). The sentence above says what this roughly corresponds to on chess.com or with FIDE. Only the moves until the game is decided count; after that there is hardly anything left to lose. For each phase you see a verdict and the accuracy, and a number only when there are enough moves. Tactics are moves in positions with a check, a threat or a winning capture; strategy, moves in quiet positions. Bots make deliberate mistakes, so their numbers come out low.
spielstaerke.letzte.erklaerung: Estimated from your last rated games against the engine (ten at most), separately for blitz, rapid and classical. Unrated games do not count. A single game says little, which is why a range is shown; it gets narrower with every game. The number follows the Lichess scale and is not a federation rating.
spielstaerke.entspricht: Your number is for {zeitklasse} and follows the Lichess scale; it corresponds to about {liste} {ziel}.
spielstaerke.entsprichtOhne: Your number is for {zeitklasse} and follows the Lichess scale; there is no comparison value for {liste}.

wertung.massstab.kurve: The curve uses the Lichess scale.
wertung.massstab.erklaerung: The “chess.com” and “FIDE” switches convert your numbers, for every time control. Blitz is compared with chess.com Blitz, rapid and classical with chess.com Rapid (chess.com has no classical rating). The basis is a comparison of many players who play on several lists (chessgoals.com, July 2026). Instead of a single number you see a range: half of the players who would have the same number here lie within it. So half lie outside, and for you alone it can be further off. FIDE has no values below about 1650; in the lower range the conversion is especially uncertain.

startseite.untertitel: A handbook for beginners and improving players
startseite.beta: The app is still a beta: it is being improved and extended continuously; it downloads updates by itself, and a tap on “Update now” activates them.
startseite.meta: Schach von Grund auf: the handbook for beginners and advancing players, with the app for the book. Every figure as a live board, the book's tools, training and an engine.
startseite.buch.text1: From the first move to the ideas that matter on the way toward 2000 Elo: the book leads from the rules and chess notation through opening principles and classical opening systems, gambits and traps, pawn structures, finding a plan and tactics, all the way to the important endgames.
startseite.buch.text2: Each chapter gives you a tool to check positions yourself. At the end, studies, annotated games and a training section bring everything together into a thinking routine for your own games.
startseite.shops.hinweis: Where to buy it will be listed here as soon as the book is published.
startseite.imBrowser.hinweis: No installation, right here in your browser. Your progress stays on this device.
startseite.training.text: For every chapter, the exercises that the box “Training zu diesem Kapitel” (Training for this chapter) in the book refers to, with up-to-date links to Lichess and other free resources.

einstellungen.schriftgroesse.hinweis: The app follows your device's text size. Here you can make it smaller or larger independently, in steps of 10 % (80 to 150 %). Applies on this device.
einstellungen.wischen.hinweis: Tapping the piece and the target square always works. A swipe only starts on a piece that is allowed to move; on all other squares the page scrolls. Applies on this device as soon as a board is opened anew.
einstellungen.zuganimation.hinweis: The moved piece glides briefly to its target square; the clock only runs on afterwards. Nothing glides after a swipe. Applies to every board opened from now on; if the device is set to reduce motion, the animation stays off.
einstellungen.startanimation: Start screen when opening the app
einstellungen.startanimation.hinweis: The golden knight from the book cover appears briefly when the app starts; a tap skips it. On phones and tablets it also appears when the app was in the background for a while. If the device is set to reduce motion, it stays off.
einstellungen.feiereffekte.hinweis: Fireworks and sparkle when you earn a medal, a badge or a record. Off: the message still appears, just without effects.
uebung.auftragZug: The task is in the book. Play your side's move on the board; the app replies with the other side's moves from the solution. Diagram in the book:
uebung.auftragDenken: You solve this exercise in your head or on paper. The task is in the book; afterwards you read the explanation here and rate yourself. Diagram in the book:
uebung.erstDenken: Think first: hints and solution appear once you have thought it over.
uebung.hinweisZug: The golden arrow shows the move.
uebung.geloest: Correct! That is the book's solution.
uebung.geloestAnders: Correct! This move is just as good. The explanation shows the book's way.
uebung.gezeigt: The book's solution is on the board. The exercise will come up for review soon.
uebung.falsch: That is not the book's move. Try again.
uebung.weiter: Correct. The other side has replied; it is your move again.
uebung.ohneErklaerung: The explanation for this exercise is still to come.
uebung.einzigerZug: Only this move reaches the goal: according to the engine, every other first move is at least one pawn worse.
uebung.eingeschaetzt: Saved. The exercise will come back for review.
training.faelligPrinzip: Like a flash-card box: every exercise from the book comes back, and every trainer task you got wrong. Solved correctly, it moves up one box and returns later: after 1, 3, 7, 16 and 35 days. Solved wrongly, it starts again and is due tomorrow.

dreissig.schritt.analyse: Analyze the previous day's game thoroughly
dreissig.ziel.taktik: Recognize patterns, wake up the Chess X-ray rule.
dreissig.ziel.partie: Apply the thinking routine under light time pressure.
dreissig.ziel.kurzanalyse: Find the first decisive mistake, not learn every computer move.
dreissig.ziel.thema: Anchor plans and technique for good.
dreissig.ziel.analyse: Turn your own mistake into an exercise: an entry in the mistake log.
dreissig.langePartie: Once a week, a long game (15+10 or longer) with a thorough analysis replaces the plan.
dreissig.weniger: Short on time? Cut the theme, never the analysis.
dreissig.taktikHinweis: Easy exercises, about two minutes each. If you get stuck: look at the solution and name the motif.
dreissig.partieHinweis: Play a game against the engine with 10 minutes per side (10 + 0, already set). Afterwards “Back” brings you here again.
dreissig.kurzanalyseHinweis: In the review, look at the curve and the marks on the board and find the first move that tips the evaluation.

maia.erklaerung: Maia is a program from the University of Toronto that learned from millions of real games how people play chess. With Maia the bots move more like humans: they more often choose the moves a person of their strength would choose, with typical plans and typical mistakes. For this the app loads an add-on package once; after that it also works without internet. With Maia most bots play somewhat stronger, and the opponent choice then shows the matching numbers.

sicherung.erklaerung: A backup is a file with everything you have done in the app: progress, games, rating, custom bots, study collection, settings and more. Keep it in a safe place. With it you move to a new device, and on the iPhone this is how your data gets from the Safari tab into the installed app. Restoring replaces all data on this device; the app asks first. If downloading does not work, use “Share backup” and send the file to yourself, for example by email. The Maia package is not included; load it again in the settings on the new device.

einstellungen.toursymbol.hinweis: The compass symbol at the top right starts the tour of the current screen. The tour of all areas is also here:
tour.haupt.willkommen: Welcome to “Schach von Grund auf”! This short tour shows you where to find everything. Tap “Next” to start, or the cross to stop at any time.
tour.haupt.buch: Book: every diagram of the book as a live board, with the book’s tools. Type the number from the book or open a chapter.
tour.haupt.training: Training: reviews that are due, your study collection and the book’s trainers for every chapter.
tour.haupt.spielen: Play: games against bots on ten levels or against a person on the same device, followed by a review of your game.
tour.haupt.nachschlagen: Reference: glossary, thinking routine, master checklist, opening profiles and all the book’s tools.
tour.haupt.einstellungen: Your profile: name and portrait, rating, progress and your games. At the top, the settings with the tabs Board, Controls, Display, Training, Bots and Help, plus the backup.
tour.haupt.symbol: This symbol sits at the top right of every screen that has a tour. A tap explains exactly that screen. You can switch it off under Profile › Settings in the “Help” tab.
tour.haupt.los: Enjoy! A good next step is to open a diagram from chapter 1 and tap the tour symbol there: the diagram screen is the heart of the app.
tour.buch.nummer: Type the number of a diagram from the book, such as 1.26, and open it. If you mistype, the app suggests matching numbers.
tour.buch.zuletzt: One tap takes you back to the diagram you opened last.
tour.buch.kapitel: The chapters of the book. The gold ring around the number shows how many diagrams you have already looked at. A tap opens the chapter with all its diagrams, trainers and exercises.
tour.buch.rundgang: You can start the tour of all areas at any time under Profile › Settings in the “Help” tab.
tour.kapitel.fortschritt: Your progress in this chapter: diagrams viewed, exercises solved, why-questions answered, learning goals ticked and your trainer passes.
tour.kapitel.trainer: The trainers for this chapter. The question mark explains how they work, the round button with the triangle ▷ starts one.
tour.kapitel.uebungen: The exercises from the book. “Solve exercises” goes through all of them, open ones first. Solved exercises come back for review later.
tour.kapitel.galerie: All diagrams as small boards, by section. Tap a section to open it, tap a board to open the diagram. A mark at the top right of a board shows that it has why-questions.
tour.kapitel.abhaken: A diagram counts as viewed after 30 seconds on screen. Here you can tick them all by hand or reset them; each section also has its own button.
tour.abbildung.nummer: The number as in the book. Tap it to open a field for jumping to any other diagram.
tour.abbildung.blaettern: Previous and next diagram in the same chapter.
tour.abbildung.zugleiste: This diagram has a move sequence. Tap a move to see the position after it, or step through half-move by half-move with the buttons below. Side lines appear under “Other moves here”.
tour.abbildung.brett: The board shows arrows and squares as in the book. You can play on at any time: tap a piece and then its target square, or swipe it. “Back to the book line” returns to the book.
tour.abbildung.werkzeugsymbole: The tools at the board, such as Count (tap a square to see its attackers and defenders), Move, Engine, X-ray and Warning signs. Each appears as soon as the book has introduced it. A second tap or a tap beside the board switches it off again. Until you have assessed the position, only Flip and Collection are here.
tour.abbildung.drehen: Flips the board so that Black is at the bottom.
tour.abbildung.sammeln: The bookmark saves the position shown, with a plan sentence and a note, to your study collection.
tour.abbildung.buendel: A bundle groups tools into one of the book's methods, such as “Check the opening” or “Finding a plan”. Here you see the bundles up to this chapter; “earlier” and “later” at the edges show the others. Slide the row sideways to see them all.
tour.abbildung.reiter: The parts of the chosen bundle. Each tab shows one tool, with its result on the board and in the card below.
tour.abbildung.karte: A tool's card shows what it found and a conclusion; “On the board” explains the markings. “View” at the top right shows the same for the other side. “How the app checks” names the book's rule. Tools can be wrong; the book is what counts.
tour.abbildung.warum: Why-questions about the position or the next move, with a choice of answers. They appear once you have looked at the diagram for 30 seconds.
tour.abbildung.engine: Play the position shown to the end against the engine.
tour.abbildung.unterschrift: The caption as in the book, with the section below. Numbers you can tap open the diagram mentioned.
tour.uebung.auftrag: The task is in the book; you solve it here. For move tasks you play on the board, and the app answers with the other side’s moves from the solution.
tour.uebung.hilfe: Think first: hints and solution appear once you have thought about it. Then graded hints help (motif, piece, move), or you can show the solution.
tour.uebung.einschaetzen: If you solve an exercise in your head, you say yourself after the explanation how it went. The exercise then comes back at growing intervals: after 1, 3, 7, 16 and 35 days.
tour.uebung.weiter: “Next exercise” takes you on through the chapter’s exercises.
tour.training.faellig: Exercises and trainer tasks that are due for review. They come back at growing intervals until they stick.
tour.training.sammlung: Your study collection: your own positions with a plan, sorted by opening, for quizzing yourself.
tour.training.website: The exercises from the book’s box “Training for this chapter” on the website, with links to Lichess. The pages work offline too.
tour.training.kapitel: Each chapter with its trainers. The heading with the number opens the chapter, the question mark explains how it works, the round button with the triangle ▷ starts. Inside a trainer, the tour symbol shows how it works.
tour.trainer.ablauf: This line sums up how the trainer works.
tour.trainer.ablaufMitte: What this trainer practises and how it works is explained at any time by the question mark on its card in the Training area.
tour.trainer.koordinaten.wahl: Four kinds of practice: find the square (against the clock, without coordinates, first with White then with Black at the bottom), write the move, play the move (castling, en passant and promotion too) and piece moves.
tour.trainer.koordinaten.notation: Notation as in the book: K, Q, R, B, N for king, queen, rook, bishop and knight, pawn moves without a letter, “x” for a capture, 0-0 and 0-0-0 for castling.
tour.trainer.runde: During a round the top line shows which task you are on and how many you got right. After each answer, “Next” takes you on.
tour.trainer.sammeln: After an answer, “Add to study collection” saves the position with a plan sentence to your own positions (Training area).
tour.trainer.ende: At the end you see your score and time. Every round counts as a pass in the chapter’s progress.
tour.trainer.roentgen.schritte: Three steps like the X-ray rule from chapter 1: your checks, your captures, then what the opponent would have if it were their move.
tour.trainer.roentgen.pfeile: Tap a piece and then its target square to draw an arrow. The same move again removes it. If there is nothing, tap “Check” straight away. Gold means found, red missed, grey does not belong.
tour.trainer.roentgen.wahl: Choose the level: easy with few arrows, hard with many checks and captures at once, or mixed.
tour.trainer.zaehlen.wahl: Two kinds of practice: count the balance on one square, and find hanging pieces against the clock.
tour.trainer.zaehlen.bilanz: Count the balance: count the attackers and defenders of the square and estimate what capturing gains in pawn units (pawn 1, knight and bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9). The app then shows the whole exchange for comparison.
tour.trainer.repertoire.wahl: Choose an opening from chapter 2 and your side.
tour.trainer.repertoire.ziehen: Play the book’s moves; the app plays the other side. A wrong move shows the book move. At key moves the app asks why it is played.
tour.trainer.zielbilanz.ausfuellen: Three goals for each side: centre, development, king safety. Choose yes, partly or no; “Check” compares with the app’s check and explains differences.
tour.trainer.abweichung.wahl: Choose an opening from chapter 2 and your side.
tour.trainer.abweichung.antworten: The engine leaves the book line. Answer according to the principles from chapters 2 and 3: centre, development, king safety. Then the app shows how the engine rates your move.
tour.trainer.faktorenbilanz.waage: Set the scales for material and time, and say who is better for king safety and activity. Then the app compares with its factor balance from chapter 3.
tour.trainer.stufe: Pick a level from 1 (easy) to 5 (hard), or all. The levels are based on how hard real players on Lichess found the puzzles.
tour.trainer.wiederholen: Tasks you got wrong come back for review later. When some are due, this button starts a round of just those.
tour.trainer.falle.entscheiden: The red arrow shows the opponent’s last move. Decide whether to take the material. Then the app shows the refutation and which warning signs from chapter 4 would have warned you.
tour.trainer.struktur.stufen: Level 1 is easy, level 5 hard: the more pawn features and pieces, the more there is to take in.
tour.trainer.struktur.schritte: Step by step: tap the strong squares, tap the weak pawns, name the kind of the gold square, then choose the matching plan sentence. “Show skeleton only” hides the pieces.
tour.trainer.planbilanz.wahl: Three kinds of practice: the three plan questions, LAP (the least active piece) and the pawn race.
tour.trainer.planbilanz.ablaufArten: Plan questions: choose one answer per question, then see the model answer. LAP: tap the piece first, then its target square. Pawn race: with opposite castling, count the moves to the first lever.
tour.trainer.taktik.wahl: Choose a motif or “mixed” and a level from 1 to 5. The levels are based on how hard real players on Lichess found the puzzles.
tour.trainer.taktik.hilfen: Play the solution on the board. If you are stuck, hints help step by step: warning sign, motif, key piece, solution. A task counts as right without a wrong move and without hints.
tour.trainer.taktik.motiv: After the solution you name the motif. That trains your eye for next time.
tour.trainer.endspiel.wahl: Choose what to practise (mating, pawn, rook or queen endings, minor pieces or a mix) and a level.
tour.trainer.endspiel.kurz: Below are short drills without an engine, such as the move into the square or the move to the opposition.
tour.trainer.endspiel.spielen: In a round you play against the engine until the goal is reached: win or hold the draw. Hints: rule of thumb, piece, move.
tour.trainer.studien.ziehen: You move, the app answers with the reply from the book. A wrong move shows the solution move as an arrow, and the engine shows why your move falls short.
tour.trainer.zugErraten.wahl: Choose a master game from chapter 11 and a side, ideally the winner’s.
tour.trainer.zugErraten.raten: Play your move and the app reveals the game move: gold the game move, red yours. If they differ, think briefly about why the master played differently.
tour.trainer.zugErraten.werkzeuge: Above the buttons you can step through the moves played. “Analyse” lets you try lines freely before you commit. “Hint: show the piece” marks the piece that moves; a hit with a hint does not count.
tour.trainer.kurzplaene.plan: Four options for little time: 5 minutes of due reviews only, 15 minutes with tactics, tactics against the clock and the daily puzzle with a streak. For the first two the app guides you step by step with a clock; the time is a guideline.
tour.trainer.dreissigMinuten.plan: Day A is game day, day B study day, in turn. The app suggests the day that is due and shows the plan with time, activity and goal.
tour.trainer.dreissigMinuten.einheit: During the session the top shows the step and the time left. The time is a guide and keeps running; “Step done” moves on. A finished session counts in your progress.
tour.trainer.fehlerdatenbank.auswertung: The analysis counts your mistakes per type over the weeks and suggests the matching trainer.
tour.trainer.fehlerdatenbank.neu: The easiest way to add a mistake is from the review of a game. Here you can also enter a position as FEN, one sentence and a mistake type from the master checklist.
tour.trainer.fehlerdatenbank.eintraege: Your entries with their positions. You can view and delete them here.
tour.trainer.denkroutine.minute: Spend one fixed minute just looking. Then enter two candidate moves and the opponent’s strongest reply to each. The app checks that every candidate has a reply and compares with the engine.
tour.lernsammlung.einleitung: This is where your own positions with a plan sentence and a note are kept. You collect them with the bookmark on any diagram, in a game review and after trainer tasks.
tour.lernsammlung.abfragen: Quiz: the app shows a position, you think of your plan, then reveal it. Done regularly, the plans stick for your games.
tour.lernsammlung.gruppen: The positions sorted by opening; each group can be quizzed on its own.
tour.lernsammlung.pgn: Copy or share as PGN: this turns the study collection into a Lichess study, each position a chapter with plan and note.
tour.lernsammlung.neu: A position from elsewhere, such as a club game: paste the FEN, write plan and note, save.
tour.nachschlagen.glossar: The glossary from the book’s appendix, with search and cross-references.
tour.nachschlagen.denkroutine: The thinking routine: four steps before every move and the tools for each phase of the game.
tour.nachschlagen.checkliste: The master checklist: what you should be able to do after each chapter, to tick off.
tour.nachschlagen.steckbriefe: The book’s opening profiles and trap checks.
tour.nachschlagen.werkzeuge: All the book’s tools by chapter: what each one checks and by which rule.
tour.glossar.suche: Type a term or part of it; the list shows matching entries at once.
tour.glossar.buchstaben: Tap a letter to jump to the terms that start with it.
tour.glossar.liste: Tap a term to open its explanation with links to related terms.
tour.begriff.karte: The explanation from the book’s appendix. Under “See also” the buttons lead to related terms; Back returns to the list.
tour.denkroutine.schritte: The four steps before every move, as in the book. The safety check before moving is part of it.
tour.denkroutine.phasen: For each phase of the game the tools you need there. Tap a phase to open it.
tour.checkliste.stand: How many points you have ticked. The ticks stay on this device and move with the backup.
tour.checkliste.karte: One card per chapter with its key question. Tap to open it: learning goals to tick, the chapter’s tool and the way to the chapter.
tour.steckbriefe.eroeffnungen: The opening profiles from chapter 2. Tap to open an entry; the button below it leads to the diagram in the book.
tour.steckbriefe.fallen: The trap checks from chapter 4: where the trap is and how to recognise it.
tour.werkzeuge.kapitel: The tools in the order of the book, one card per chapter. Tap a name to see what the tool shows and which rule it uses.
tour.ich.profilkarte: Your name and your portrait, both optional. They appear in your games. The pencil on the right (at first the “Name and portrait” button) opens the choice: pick a picture, design your own or no picture.
tour.ich.wertung: Your rating from rated games, with its history. The tabs show your estimated strength per game phase instead. Below you choose whether you see the last games or a period.
tour.ich.fortschritt: Your progress through the whole book: figures viewed, learning goals ticked, trainers you have done at least once, and ready-made bots beaten per time class. “By chapter” opens the chapter list; tap a chapter to open it.
tour.ich.reiterBrett: Board: colours and wood, the piece set with preview, and the coordinates.
tour.ich.reiterAnzeige: Display: night mode, text size and language.
tour.ich.reiterBots: Bots: with the Maia add-on, the bots choose the moves people of their strength would play. You load it once; after that it works offline. Here you load it, switch it on or off and delete it.
tour.ich.daten: Your data stays on this device only. Back it up as a file now and then; the file also lets you move to another device.
tour.ich.ueber: App version, data version and whether the app is ready offline. “Report a bug” sends the author a bug, a wish or an error in the book, with these details if you like.
tour.spielen.laufend: Your game in progress. A tap takes you back to the board; the clock is paused while you are away.
tour.spielen.start: Where the game starts: the initial position, a figure from the book or a position of your own. “Set up position” opens a board for placing the pieces, or you paste a FEN.
tour.spielen.einstellungen: Here you choose the time control and, against the engine, your colour. With a clock, the game belongs to a time class (bullet, blitz, rapid, classical); rating and stars count separately per time class. A “Rated game” exists only against the engine from the starting position. It counts for your rating, but without aids and takebacks.
tour.spielen.hilfen: Playing aids for unrated games: takebacks, the book's tools on the board and warnings about big mistakes.
tour.spielen.eroeffnung: From the starting position your opponent opens like humans of its strength. Here you can instead give it an opening from the book or a well-known opening; it follows it as long as you play its moves. Or it plays the opening entirely on its own.
tour.spielen.gegner: The kind of opponent: “Custom level” (you set the strength for each phase, style and mistakes yourself), “Ready-made bots” (opponents with an Elo number and their own style, sorted by level, plus the “For fun” group) or “Custom bots” (opponents you create yourself).
tour.spielen.gegnerart: Who you play against: the engine, or human against human, both sides on the same device.
tour.spielen.sprechblase: The chosen opponent introduces itself: strength, style and the mistakes it likes to make.
tour.spielen.gitter: The opponents by level; tap a level to open it. A star shows that you have already beaten a bot in a rated game in this time class. Once you have beaten every bot of a level, its group mode unlocks: then they play against you together.
tour.spielen.eigene: Create your own opponents here: name, portrait, strength per phase, playing style, typical mistakes and blind spots. You can edit or delete saved opponents.
tour.spielen.beginnen: The bar at the bottom sums up your choice (opponent, colour, time control, rated). “Start” begins the game; if one is already running, you are asked first.
tour.spielen.spielstaerke: Your playing strength from your latest rated games, with a range. The more games, the narrower it gets.
tour.spielen.partien: Your games. A tap opens a game with its review. “Import a game (PGN)” brings in a game from elsewhere for a review.
tour.spielen.filter: “Filter” narrows the list (result, rating, colour, opponent, time control), the second button sorts it. Active filters appear below; the × removes one.
tour.partie.zuege: The moves of the game. Tap a move to see the position after it; tap the last move to return to the current position.
tour.partie.uhr: Both clocks, if the game has a time control. Each clock is on its player's side of the board; against the engine, yours is at the bottom.
tour.partie.brett: This is where you move: tap a piece and then the target square, or swipe the piece. After the game, the board shows arrows for the better move in the review.
tour.partie.brettwerkzeuge: At the board: Count, Engine, X-ray and the warning signs W1–W7, if the aids allow them, plus Flip. A second tap switches a tool off.
tour.partie.ruhig: The eye switches on the calm view: only board and clocks, without tools and texts.
tour.partie.werkzeuge: The book's methods as bundles for your game, if the aids allow them. In rated games they are off.
tour.partie.status: Whose move it is, plus “Take back” (if allowed) and “Resign”.
tour.partie.ende: The result. From here you play the same position again or start a new game.
tour.partie.auswertung: After the game the engine checks every move. The bar shows its progress; you can start reading meanwhile.
tour.partie.kurve: The evaluation graph: who stood better when. Slide your finger along it to step through the moves; the buttons zoom in on a phase.
tour.partie.staerke: How accurately you played and roughly how strong that was, overall and per phase. Plus your moves by kind, such as mistakes or blunders, compared with players of your strength. The switch at the top changes between your moves and your opponent's.
tour.partie.abweichung: The first move where you clearly left the best path, with a jump to that point.
tour.partie.patzer: Your mistakes and blunders, to expand. A tap jumps to the move.
tour.partie.rueckblick: The card for the move shown: how good it was, what would have been better and how the opponent punishes a mistake. For a theory move, tapping “opening” lists the openings it belongs to. From here the position goes into the mistake database or the study collection.
tour.partie.pgn: The game as PGN to copy or share, for example for an analysis on Lichess.
spielstaerke.keineZuege: This side has not made a move yet.
zugklassen.erklaerung: Each row counts one kind of move, such as good moves, mistakes or blunders; the box shows how many you played. The bar compares this with players of a strength of about {elo}: the dark line is the usual value, the grey zone is “normal”. For good moves many is good, for weak ones few. “▸” means far above the usual. Theory moves are known opening moves. For a bot, the comparison uses its own rating.
zugklassen.zuWenig: A comparison with the usual needs at least 15 of your own moves; until then only the counts are shown.
stil.angreifer.text: looks for checks and moves close to your king.
stil.positionsspieler.text: avoids checks and king attacks, keeps the tension and builds up calmly.
stil.taktiker.text: likes to capture and move forward and dislikes retreats.
stil.verteidiger.text: captures less, would rather retreat than advance and keeps the position together.
stil.draufgaenger.text: storms forward with pawns and pieces and avoids trades.
stil.vereinfacher.text: likes to trade pieces and prefers to leave the pawns where they are.
stil.universell.text: no preference, like most players of the same strength.
spielen.stilnetz.hinweis: Tap the points on the spokes: the further out, the stronger the style; the outermost point goes beyond real players. You can mix several styles, but not two opposites on the same line: then the one you chose last applies. Tapping the same point again removes the style, the centre resets to “All-rounder”. A style only decides between roughly equally good moves.
spielen.eigene.menschlich.keineNeigungTe: No error type and no blind spot is set: the bot plays like the pure level without extra mistakes. No human of that strength does.
spielen.eigene.menschlich.anteil: About {anteil} of players at this strength are at least this unusual in every setting (a rough estimate).
spielen.eigene.menschlich.unmenschlichTe: {anzahl} sliders are outside what real players at this strength do.
spielen.eigene.richtung.staerker: The sliders make it rather stronger than the number shown, because it makes its mistakes less often than humans. Only a measurement shows by how much.
spielen.eigene.richtung.schwaecher: The sliders make it rather weaker than the number shown, because it makes its mistakes more often than humans. Only a measurement shows by how much.
spielen.eigene.richtung.gleich: On average it makes its mistakes as often as humans. The number from the levels remains the best estimate.
spielen.profil.erklaerung: How often it makes each kind of mistake, compared with humans of its strength. “Normal” means as often as usual. “Very rarely” and “very often” are rare among real players. “Off”: it never makes this mistake.
spielen.profil.fleckenHinweis: Kinds of moves it overlooks, in five groups. Tap a point to set the group: inside off, then very rarely to very often.
spielen.profil.regler.eroeffnungsfehler: Opening mistakes (early queen, lost tempo, pawn grabbing)
spielen.profil.fleckgruppe.ruhig.satz: misses quiet moves when a capture is possible.
spielen.profil.fleckgruppe.bauer.satz: misses what a quiet pawn move does.
spielen.profil.fleckgruppe.fernwirkung.s: misses bishops, rooks and the queen at a distance, including X-ray attacks through pieces.
spielen.profil.fleckgruppe.wendungen.sat: misses in-between moves, discovered attacks and back-rank weaknesses.
spielen.profil.fleckenKeine: No blind spots: sees everything its level sees.
spielen.profil.normalLegende: Dashed ring “normal”: like humans of this strength.
spielen.profil.fein: Fine controls for each mistake type
spielen.profil.feinWarnung: With the box ticked you set each kind of mistake separately. The chart, presets and maximum loss are then locked and show an average. If you untick the box and tap the chart, the new value applies again to all mistakes on that spoke.
