spielen.eroeffnungPraxis: The bot opens like humans of its strength: it chooses the moves real players of its strength play here on Lichess. If the game deviates or a move would be very rare, it thinks for itself. Theoreticians stay with the known moves longer, hasty players leave them sooner.
spielen.eroeffnungPraxisLinie: The bot follows this opening from practice as long as you play its moves; afterwards it keeps opening like humans of its strength.
spielen.staerkewahl.erklaerung: What real players of a given strength choose most often, counted over one month on Lichess. Pick the bands: each band adds the three most frequent openings not yet in the list. A tap sets the opening; the bot follows it as long as you play its moves.

fundstueck.album.erklaerung: Sometimes a find is waiting at the end of a training round: a story, a curious fact or a rule of thumb from the book. At most one a day; exactly when stays a surprise.
fundstueck.text.chaturanga: Chess probably comes from India: around the 6th century people played chaturanga there, with foot soldiers, horses, elephants and chariots.
fundstueck.text.schah-mat: Via Persia the game reached the Arab world. The Persian word “shah” for king gave us the word chess; “shah mat” means roughly: the king is helpless.
fundstueck.text.dame-neu: For a long time the queen was the weakest piece and moved only one square diagonally. Only towards the end of the 15th century, in Spain, did she gain today's power, and the game became much faster.
fundstueck.text.alfil: The bishop used to be called the alfil, the elephant. It jumped exactly two squares diagonally, even over other pieces.
fundstueck.text.lewis: The Lewis chessmen were carved in the 12th century, mostly from walrus ivory. They were found in 1831 on the Scottish island of Lewis.
fundstueck.text.london-1851: The first major international tournament took place in London in 1851. It was won by Adolf Anderssen from Breslau.
fundstueck.text.unsterbliche: Anderssen played the “Immortal Game” against Lionel Kieseritzky in London in 1851, a casual game outside the tournament. He gave up both rooks and his queen and still delivered mate.
fundstueck.text.immergruene: Anderssen won the “Evergreen Game” against Jean Dufresne in Berlin in 1852, with a combination that is still admired today.
fundstueck.text.morphy: Paul Morphy from New Orleans travelled to Europe in 1858 and beat almost all the leading players. Soon afterwards he withdrew from chess.
fundstueck.text.oper: Morphy played his best-known game in 1858 in a box at the Paris Opera, against the Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard, while the singers performed on stage.
fundstueck.text.steinitz: Wilhelm Steinitz became the first official world champion in 1886, after a match against Johannes Zukertort.
fundstueck.text.lasker: Emanuel Lasker was world champion for 27 years, from 1894 to 1921, longer than anyone else.
fundstueck.text.capablanca: José Raúl Capablanca learned chess as a small child by watching his father play. Shortly afterwards he is said to have beaten him.
fundstueck.text.botwinnik: Mikhail Botvinnik was world champion three times: twice he lost the title and won it back in a return match.
fundstueck.text.menchik: Vera Menchik became the first women's world champion in 1927 and held the title until her death in 1944.
fundstueck.text.fide: The world chess federation FIDE was founded in Paris in 1924. Its motto, in Latin, means: we are one family.
fundstueck.text.olympiade: The first official Chess Olympiad was held in London in 1927. Since then teams from all over the world have played there.
fundstueck.text.schachuhr: Chess clocks with two clockworks appeared towards the end of the 19th century. Before that, a player could think about a single move for hours.
fundstueck.text.notation: In English-speaking countries moves were long written in descriptive notation, such as “P-K4” for e4. Since 1981 FIDE has recognised only algebraic notation.
fundstueck.text.elo: The Elo rating is named after the physicist Arpad Elo, who developed the method. FIDE introduced it in 1970.
fundstueck.text.schachtuerke: The “Mechanical Turk” of 1770 looked like a machine that played chess. In reality a strong player sat hidden inside the cabinet.
fundstueck.text.deep-blue: In 1997 world champion Garry Kasparov lost a six-game match to the computer Deep Blue. A year earlier he had still won.
fundstueck.text.reykjavik: In 1972 Bobby Fischer became world champion in Reykjavík against Boris Spassky. The match was followed all over the world.
fundstueck.text.polgar: Judit Polgár became a grandmaster in 1991 at the age of 15, younger than Bobby Fischer had been. She played almost only against men and beat several world champions.
fundstueck.text.philidor: In the 18th century François-André Danican Philidor was both a chess master and an opera composer. He wrote that pawns are the soul of chess.
fundstueck.text.ruy-lopez: The Spanish Opening (Ruy Lopez) is named after Ruy López de Segura, a Spanish priest who published a chess book in 1561.
fundstueck.text.greco: In the 17th century Gioachino Greco wrote down games with quick mates. Many of them still turn up today as opening traps.
fundstueck.text.stroebeck: Ströbeck in the Harz mountains is called the chess village: chess has been cherished there for centuries, and it has been a school subject since 1823.
fundstueck.text.fernschach: In correspondence chess, moves used to be sent by postcard. A move often took days to arrive, and some games lasted for years.
fundstueck.text.carlsen: In 2014 Magnus Carlsen reached an Elo rating of 2882, higher than anyone before him.
fundstueck.text.zwanzig-zuege: White has 20 possible first moves: 16 pawn moves and 4 knight moves. Black has the same, so after the first pair of moves there are 400 positions.
fundstueck.text.85-milliarden: After four moves by each side there are already almost 85 billion possible ways the game can have gone.
fundstueck.text.shannon: In 1950 Claude Shannon estimated the number of possible chess games at about 10 to the power of 120, far more than there are atoms in the observable universe.
fundstueck.text.laengste-moeglich: Because of the fifty-move rule no game can last forever. The longest possible game has just under 6000 moves.
fundstueck.text.laengste-turnier: The longest tournament game between masters was played by Nikolić and Arsović in Belgrade in 1989: 269 moves, more than 20 hours, and in the end a draw.
fundstueck.text.narrenmatt: The fastest possible mate is called Fool's Mate: 1. f3 e5 2. g4 Qh4#. White is mated after two moves.
fundstueck.text.roesselsprung: A knight can travel across the whole board and land on every square exactly once. The mathematician Leonhard Euler already studied such knight's tours.
fundstueck.text.acht-damen: Eight queens can be placed on the board so that none attacks another. There are exactly 92 ways to do it.
fundstueck.text.neun-damen: One side can have up to nine queens in a game: the original one and eight promoted pawns.
fundstueck.text.unterverwandlung: A pawn may also promote to a knight, bishop or rook. Usually the queen is right, but sometimes only a rook avoids stalemate, or only a knight gives check.
fundstueck.text.rochade: Castling is the only move in which two of your own pieces move at once: king and rook.
fundstueck.text.en-passant: En passant arose when pawns were allowed to move two squares on their first move. That way a pawn cannot slip past an enemy pawn unpunished.
fundstueck.text.patt-england: Stalemate was not always a draw. In England, in roughly the 17th and 18th centuries, it counted as a loss for the player who gave stalemate.
fundstueck.text.tote-stellung: King against king is an immediate draw, and so is king and bishop against king: mate is impossible there.
fundstueck.text.zwei-springer: Two knights alone cannot force mate against a bare king. It only works if the defender helps.
fundstueck.text.weiss-rechts: The board is set up correctly when the bottom right square is light. At the start the queen stands on a square of her own colour.
fundstueck.text.halbes-brett: At the start there are 32 pieces on 64 squares: exactly half the board is occupied.
fundstueck.text.blindschach: Strong players can play blindfold, without looking at the board. Some manage dozens of games at once this way.
fundstueck.text.handy-engine: A chess program on an ordinary phone today plays stronger than any world champion.
fundstueck.text.tablebase: For every position with up to seven pieces it has been worked out how it ends with best play. Some of these wins take more than 500 moves.
fundstueck.text.schach960: In Chess960 the pieces on the back rank are shuffled. That gives 960 starting positions and hardly any memorised openings.
fundstueck.text.springer-rand: A knight in the centre reaches up to eight squares, on the edge at most four, and in the corner only two.
fundstueck.text.entwicklung: Bring out the minor pieces first, then the queen. Every opening move should do something new.
fundstueck.text.zentrum: Whoever controls the centre has more room for their pieces and reaches both wings faster.
fundstueck.text.figurenwerte: Pawn 1, knight and bishop about 3, rook 5, queen 9: a rule of thumb for counting. The position can overturn it.
fundstueck.text.schlagreflex: Not every capture has to be recaptured at once. A quick look for something better pays off.
fundstueck.text.rochieren: Castling early brings the king to safety and the rook into play.
fundstueck.text.vergifteter-bauer: An offered pawn may be poisoned. First check what happens after you take it.
fundstueck.text.fianchetto: A bishop on g2 or b2 looks along the whole long diagonal into the opponent's camp.
fundstueck.text.gambit: A gambit gives up material for time and activity. You have to use the lead before the opponent catches up.
fundstueck.text.falle-geschenk: Before every move ask: what does my opponent want? A trap often looks like a gift.
fundstueck.text.bauern-zurueck: Pawns never move backwards. Every pawn move changes the position for good, so think it over.
fundstueck.text.isolani: An isolated pawn often gives active play, but in the endgame it easily becomes a weakness.
fundstueck.text.vorposten: A knight on a square that no enemy pawn can attack any more is often superbly placed.
fundstueck.text.bauerninseln: Fewer pawn islands are usually better: connected pawns protect each other.
fundstueck.text.zwei-schwaechen: One weakness can often be defended; two far apart usually cannot.
fundstueck.text.prophylaxe: First ask what your opponent is planning, then make your own plan.
fundstueck.text.gabel: Where two pieces stand undefended, it pays to look for a fork.
fundstueck.text.fesselung: A pinned piece is a poor defender. Attack it again.
fundstueck.text.ueberlastung: A piece with two jobs can often do neither of them properly.
fundstueck.text.zwischenzug: Before recapturing, check whether a check or a threat fits in first.
fundstueck.text.grundreihe: A king without an escape square can be mated on the back rank. A small pawn move at the right time helps.
fundstueck.text.koenig-aktiv: In the endgame the king becomes a strong piece: it belongs in the centre.
fundstueck.text.quadratregel: If the king can reach the square of a passed pawn, it catches the pawn.
fundstueck.text.opposition: When the kings face each other with one square between them, the side to move often has to give way.
fundstueck.text.zugzwang: Sometimes every move is a bad move: whoever has to move then makes their position worse.
fundstueck.text.tarrasch: Rooks belong behind passed pawns, both your own and your opponent's.
fundstueck.text.brueckenbau: By building a bridge, the rook shields its king from checks so the pawn can get through.
fundstueck.text.philidor-stellung: In a rook endgame the defender often holds the draw by keeping the rook on the third rank until the pawn advances.
fundstueck.text.ungleichfarbige: Endgames with opposite-coloured bishops often end in a draw, even with an extra pawn.
fundstueck.text.kandidaten: First collect several candidate moves, then calculate. The first idea is not always the best.
fundstueck.text.eigene-fehler: You learn most from your own mistakes: write them down, understand them, repeat.
fundstueck.text.sicherheitsblick: Before letting go of the piece, check briefly whether the move hangs anything.

rivale.spruch.angreifer.remis: My attack fizzled out, but I didn't lose either.
rivale.spruch.angreifer.botNiederlage: Well played! You coolly beat off my attack.
rivale.spruch.vorsichtig.begruessung: First I make everything safe. Then we'll see.
rivale.spruch.vorsichtig.remis: A draw. Better safe than sorry, I always say.
rivale.spruch.vorsichtig.botNiederlage: Well played! All my caution didn't help this time.
rivale.spruch.materialist.botSieg: One pawn up, and off it goes. Another game?
rivale.spruch.materialist.remis: A draw? But I was a pawn up …
rivale.spruch.materialist.botNiederlage: Well played! That pawn was poisoned after all.
rivale.spruch.taktiker.begruessung: Watch your pieces. I see every fork.
rivale.spruch.taktiker.botSieg: One little combination and it was over. Rematch?
rivale.spruch.taktiker.remis: A draw. My tactics didn't fire this time.
rivale.spruch.taktiker.botNiederlage: Well played! You saw through my tricks.
rivale.spruch.stratege.begruessung: A good plan beats any trap. Do you have one?
rivale.spruch.stratege.botSieg: Step by step, as planned. Want to try again?
rivale.spruch.stratege.remis: A draw. Our plans cancelled each other out.
rivale.spruch.stratege.botNiederlage: Well played! Your plan was better than mine today.
rivale.spruch.hektiker.begruessung: Quick, quick, no time to lose!
rivale.spruch.hektiker.remis: A draw! Phew, that all went so fast.
rivale.spruch.hektiker.botNiederlage: Well played! I was too hasty again.
rivale.spruch.damenfan.begruessung: My queen is looking forward to meeting you.
rivale.spruch.damenfan.botSieg: The queen fixed it again. Another one?
rivale.spruch.damenfan.remis: A draw. Not even my queen found a way.
rivale.spruch.damenfan.botNiederlage: Well played! My poor queen came out too early.
rivale.spruch.koenigswanderer.begruessun: Castle? Maybe later. My king likes the centre.
rivale.spruch.koenigswanderer.botSieg: See, my king was quite comfortable in the centre.
rivale.spruch.koenigswanderer.remis: A draw. My king enjoyed a nice walk.
rivale.spruch.koenigswanderer.botNiederl: Well played! I should have castled after all.
rivale.spruch.traeumer.begruessung: I dream of a beautiful sacrifice. Maybe today?
rivale.spruch.traeumer.botSieg: A dream of a game! Will you play another one?
rivale.spruch.traeumer.remis: A draw. The beautiful move never came.
rivale.spruch.traeumer.botNiederlage: Well played! I daydreamed right past the quiet move.
rivale.spruch.endspieler.begruessung: Go ahead and trade. I'll wait for you in the endgame.
rivale.spruch.endspieler.botSieg: I know my way around endgames. Rematch?
rivale.spruch.endspieler.remis: A draw. An honest endgame, down to the last pawn.
rivale.spruch.endspieler.botNiederlage: Well played! You never let it get to the endgame.
rivale.spruch.theoretiker.begruessung: I know lots of openings. Which one do you play?
rivale.spruch.theoretiker.botSieg: Well prepared is half won. Another game?
rivale.spruch.theoretiker.remis: A draw. That wasn't in any book.
rivale.spruch.theoretiker.botNiederlage: Well played! After the opening I was at my wit's end.
